title: Distilling Feedback into Memory-as-a-Tool
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the problem of repeatedly paying the full inference-time cost of self-correction and critique in large language models. The authors argue that iterative refinement methods such as self-critique are effective but ephemeral: the model improves only within a single interaction, and the learning signal is lost when the context resets.

To address this, the paper proposes a Memory-as-a-Tool framework that converts transient evaluator feedback into persistent, file-based memory entries. Instead of storing raw interaction logs, the model abstracts feedback into generalizable guidelines, saves them to a /memories/ directory, and later retrieves relevant notes before answering similar tasks. The system is evaluated on the new Rubric Feedback Bench, which includes rubric-based writing, behavioral, and ethical reasoning tasks, and is compared against zero-shot and inference-time self-critique baselines.

The empirical setting is not a K-12 educational intervention but an LLM benchmark using frontier models such as Claude Sonnet 4.5, GPT-5.1, and Gemini 3 Pro. Across short continual-learning sequences and a longer mixed-task horizon, the memory-augmented approach is reported to match or exceed self-critique performance while substantially reducing cost. The main conclusion is that distilling feedback into persistent memory can amortize reasoning costs and support continual adaptation across tasks.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a conference paper with a clearly described evaluation protocol, but it is not a K-12 study and does not use a randomized or quasi-experimental educational design. The evidence is primarily benchmark-based and computational, so it fits a lower internal-validity category for the education evidence framework.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported gains are meaningful for model performance and cost efficiency, including a clear advantage in rubric-score trajectories and a lower-cost Pareto frontier. However, the impact is indirect for K-12 education because the study is on synthetic/open-ended writing tasks rather than teachers, students, or classroom implementation.

interventions.use_case: memory-augmented large language model agents that use rubric-based feedback, file-based read/write memory, and self-critique to improve generated responses across sequential tasks

finding.finding_summary: The paper evaluates rubric-based writing tasks and finds that the memory-augmented LLM improves writing quality over time. In continual-learning experiments across 15 examples per model (H=3 per category), the Memory + Feedback approach rapidly matched or exceeded the self-critique baseline after about two feedback rounds; in a long-horizon mixed-task setting (H=12), the memory agent achieved 0.78 ± 0.10 versus 0.52 ± 0.25 without memory on final task scores.
finding.measure: Judge scores on rubric-based writing tasks / open-ended text generation quality
finding.study_size: n=15 per model in continual-learning evaluation; n=12 in long-horizon mixed-task experiment

finding.finding_summary: A central result is that distilling feedback into persistent memory substantially reduces inference-time cost relative to repeated self-critique. The paper reports that Memory + Feedback achieves performance comparable to iterative self-correction while keeping the cost profile much closer to zero-shot generation, because critique is paid for once and retrieval is cheap thereafter.
finding.measure: Average cost per task and cost-score Pareto frontier
